newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ debt rallies a touch, cash helps short end.
newsitem.headline: NZ debt rallies a touch, cash helps short end.

text.p: Figures in brackets compare against previous day's close
FUTURES PHYSICAL YIELD (PCT)
90-DAY BILLS (SEP) 93.13 (PREV 93.10) 90-DAYS 6.90 (PREV 6.93)
OVERNIGHT CASH 6.50 PCT (PREV 6.50) US 5-YR 6.31 (PREV 6.27)
NZ MCI -0.91 (PREV -0.85)
* NZ debt ends stronger across curve in face of US weakness
* Lower cash rate seen helping short end hold in well
* Volumes minimal but some offshore buying interest
New Zealand debt securities finished stronger across the curve on Wednesday as offshore buying interest rescued the local market from the weakness seen in U.S. Treasuries.
The 02/01 bond rallied four basis points to 6.83 percent, while the long bond was down three in yield to 7.06 percent.
Dealers said the session had not been riveting. A Wellington trader said there had been some offshore interest to buy NZ debt securities but flows were minimal.

"I think as we grind closer to the budget and the monetary policy statement (MPS) we will probably trade in our own right. We'll divorce ourselves from the Aussie and U.S. markets over the next few days, I would think," he added.
The National-NZ First coalition government's first budget, for 1997/98, is due next Thursday, while the RBNZ's MPS is the following day.
Dealers expect the RBNZ to sanction an easing in monetary conditions from the levels assumed by the bank in March, but opinion is divided over how much of an easing is in the pipeline.
At present the market is holding conditions 91 basis points (in interest rate terms) below the RBNZ's latest assumptions.

Dealers said the short end held in well during Wednesday's session, with the 90-day bank bills rallying three basis points to 6.90 percent. The currency's Trade-Weighted Index finished at 67.57, from its 67.64 close on Tuesday.
"I thought the 90-day bills might have drifted slightly higher towards seven percent, but it was not to be at this stage," one dealer said.
"Cash is probably a bit of a driver -- it's trading around 6.50 percent, so there's a bit of cash and carry for guys holding assets."
